scope: Fourth expansion batch: nine controlled verb-form exercises, three each for the immediately-before, ongoing and just-completed stages with tokoro. Each stage uses eating lunch, writing a letter and reading a novel. Other tokoro constructions, stative/resultative predicates and independent bakari exercises are outside this batch.

sources.publisher: The Japan Foundation, Minna no Kyozai
sources.section: BMA00036, structure diagrams and basic explanations A-C: dictionary form, teiru and ta before tokoro desu. Teacher notes: activity predicates; comparison with tabakari; past reference points and other tokoro constructions.

sources.publisher: Tae Kim's Guide to Learning Japanese
sources.section: Using teiru for enduring states: omitting i in conversational Japanese, including the note on polite speech. Enduring state-of-being vs enduring state of action: why teiru is not always an ongoing action.

authoringNotes: Examples are newly authored rather than copied source exercises. Sources support grammatical patterns, not a claim that the new contexts are automatically ambiguity-free.
The three temporal stages are related constructions, not three copies of the same label. Each exercise still has one canonical answer and one SRS identity.

The question-side English explicitly requests the given verb's dictionary, teiru or ta form and permits contractions. Tokoro desu is already printed. Answers contain only the missing verb form, with kana spellings and conversational teiru/deiru contractions accepted.

The constraints are visible before answering, not hidden in evidence or feedback. They avoid an unrestricted cloze that would falsely reject natural replacements such as tabakari, tsumori or a longer completion phrase.

Screen against the whole linked article while respecting the visible controlled-task instruction. Other constructions may describe the same situation in another sentence; the feedback must not label them globally invalid.

The selected predicates describe activities with clear contextual starts and completions. Do not transfer this three-stage interpretation mechanically to every occurrence of teiru or every tokoro construction.
The before/during/after examples share three lexical frames so each verb occurs at every stage, rather than letting a particular verb predict the target.
The original 47 exercise records remain unchanged. The new section does not claim complete coverage of tokoro, bakari or the article's full inventory.
